title: Dativ i lokativ
theme: Dajem Ani kahvu shows giving to someone, sitting at a place, and in versus into.
reviewerNotes: Pedagogy polish after Fact Checker. Preserved Bosnian-editor dative/locative forms (Ani/Emiru/Amiri/kući/kuću/kahvi/mostu/Sarajevu). Vocab heads confirmed dictionary/list forms. whyHere.heading: Why you are here
whyHere.body: Today you learn the to, at, and about job on the same coffee and house. Emir can give coffee to Ana, and Ana can already sit in Sarajevo. English hangs to and in in front. Bosnian hangs the job on the end, and it uses one shared outfit for giving to someone and being at a place. You also learn why into the house and in the house are not the same ending.

englishLies.heading: Why English lies
englishLies.body: English lies because the lines I give coffee to Ana and I am in the house keep Ana and house still. Little words do the work. Bosnian dresses the person you give to and the place you sit in. Ana becomes Ani, and kuća becomes kući. Schools split the labels into dativ for to and lokativ for at and about. On these words the ending is usually the same, so you can learn one chart and two English jobs.

knownLine.heading: A line you already say
knownLine.body: Book 1 already parked you in the city with U Sarajevu, which means in Sarajevo. That u on Sarajevu is today’s at job on a leftover place-word. The new twin is giving. Emir says Dajem Ani kahvu, which means I give Ana coffee. Ani is to Ana. Kahvu is still the want-it form from Chapter 2 for the thing being handed over. Two jobs can sit in one short line.
knownLine.speaker: Emir

pattern.heading: The pattern
pattern.body: She-pile words swap that final a for i in the to, at, and about job. Kahva becomes kahvi, kuća becomes kući, and Ana becomes Ani. He-pile words usually take u, so most becomes mostu and Emir becomes Emiru. Leftover-pile words usually take u too, so pivo becomes pivu and Sarajevo becomes Sarajevu. Use that form when you give to someone, when liking uses a to-me scrap like mi, when you are in or on a place, and when you talk about a thing. Keep the want-it form for motion into a place.

howYouGuess.heading: The pests
howYouGuess.body: The big pest is in versus into. Ja sam u kući means I am in the house, with today’s at form. Idem u kuću means I go into the house, with the want-it form from Chapter 2. The little word u stays the same while the house ending shows the job. The second pest is giving to Ana while leaving her as Ana. Dajem Ana kahvu is English word order with a Bosnian costume. She needs the to form Ani. The third pest is thinking to and at need two different endings on these words. They usually share one outfit.

trick.heading: The bit that tricks you
trick.body: The trap is to hear u and always reach for one ending. U is not the job. The job sits on the next word. Motion into a place wants the want-it form. Being in or at a place wants today’s form. The other trap is to mark the gift and forget the person. In Dajem Ani kahvu, Ani is to Ana, and kahvu is the coffee being given. If you only change coffee, you still missed the to job.

nerd.heading: Why it's like this
nerd.body:
Old English is the English of England about a thousand years ago, not a class you missed. Farmers and priests around Winchester marked to and at on thing-words and on people words. You still own scraps when you say him and them instead of he and they. Coffee and house lost those outfits in later English. You speak the later version.

Bosnian kept the outfits. The to job and the at job often wear the same ending on one word in the singular, which is why Ani and kući feel like one chart with two English uses. Schools still print two labels. Your ear can treat them as one shared suit until a later chapter needs a finer split.

items.prompt: Emir gives coffee to Ana. Which form of Ana?
You are in the house. Which form?
You go into the house. Which form?
items.explanation: Into takes the want-it form kuću.

items.prompt: We are in Sarajevo. Which form?
items.explanation: U Sarajevu. At form on leftover.

items.prompt: Amira gives beer to Emir. Which form of Emir?
items.explanation: To Emir is Emiru. Emira was the Chapter 2 people pest for seeing him.

items.prompt: Talking about coffee. Which form after o?
items.explanation: O kahvi. About uses today’s form.

items.prompt: Standing on the bridge. Which form after na?
items.explanation: Na mostu. At form on he-pile most.

items.prompt: Someone says Dajem Ana kahvu. What went wrong?
options: Ana needs the to form Ani.
items.explanation: The gift kahvu is fine. The person needs Ani.

items.prompt: Why do u kući and u kuću differ?
options: One is leftover and one is she
In and into are different jobs
Kući is leftover and kuću is she
items.explanation: The little word u stays the same, but the house takes a different job ending.

items.prompt: Do to and at need two different endings on Ana and kuća today?
options: No, these words usually share one outfit for both English jobs
items.explanation: One chart covers both English uses of to and at on these words.

questions.question: Sviđa mi se Sarajevo. What is mi doing?
options: Marking the experiencer in the to job
questions.explanation: Sviđa mi se uses the to job on mi for the person who likes it. Sarajevo stays name-it.

questions.question: Dajem Ani kahvu. What is Ani?
questions.explanation: Ani is the to form. Kahvu is the gift.

questions.question: Ja sam u kući versus Idem u kuću. What changed?
options: In uses kući. Into uses kuću.
questions.explanation: Little word u stays. The house ending shows the job.

questions.question: Why does U Sarajevu look right in Book 1?
options: It is the of form from Chapter 3
It is the at form on leftover Sarajevo
questions.explanation: Sarajevu is today’s at outfit. Sarajeva was from.

questions.question: Pričam o kahvi uses which job?
questions.explanation: O takes the about form kahvi.

questions.question: What comes next?
options: Seven jobs dumped on one page with no map
With, calling, and one preposition map
questions.explanation: Chapter 5 closes the case map with instrumental and vocative.

next.body: You now know why Ani and kući share an outfit for to and at, and why into still borrows the want-it form. U Sarajevu and Dajem Ani kahvu are the same family. Chapter 5 adds with and calling, then hangs one preposition map for the whole job set. You still will not drown in a naked seven-row dump.
